proofs.proof_tex:
The total population size is \(2k+4k=6k\).  Therefore a size-two
block has
\[
 w_l=\frac2{6k}=\frac1{3k},\qquad q_l=2^{-2}=\frac14,
\]
and a size-four block has
\[
 w_l=\frac4{6k}=\frac2{3k},\qquad q_l=2^{-4}=\frac1{16},
\]
where the reveal probabilities follow from balanced independent
assignment.  Direct substitution in the definitions of \(S\) and
\(M\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 S
 &=k\frac{(1/(3k))^2}{1/4}
   +k\frac{(2/(3k))^2}{1/16}
   =\frac4{9k}+\frac{64}{9k}
   =\frac{68}{9k},\\
 M
 &=\max\left\{\frac{1/(3k)}{1/4},
                \frac{2/(3k)}{1/16}\right\}
   =\frac{32}{3k}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{17}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \frac{M\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}}{\sqrt S}
 =\frac{32\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}}{\sqrt{68k}}
 \longrightarrow0
\tag{18}
\]
for fixed \(\alpha\).  The hypothesis of
\(\mathrm{thm{:}no\text{-}dominance\text{-}upper}\) therefore holds
eventually, and substitution of (17) in that theorem gives the stated
upper bound.

Finally, the cap breakpoints in
\(\mathrm{def{:}capped\text{-}modulus}\) are \(q_l/w_l\).  They equal
\[
 \frac{1/4}{1/(3k)}=\frac{3k}{4},
 \qquad
 \frac{1/16}{2/(3k)}=\frac{3k}{32}.
\tag{19}
\]
Because \(r\mapsto2^{-r}\) is injective on positive integers, a
single common block size cannot yield both \(1/4\) and \(1/16\); (19)
also shows directly that it cannot yield both breakpoint values.

The blocks form a partition and each has cardinality \(r\), so
\(n=Lr\) and hence \(L=n/r\).  Balanced independent assignment gives
\(q_l=2^{-r}\), while the weight definition gives \(w_l=r/n\).
Therefore
\[
 S=\sum_{l=1}^L\frac{w_l^2}{q_l}
 =\frac nr\frac{r^2}{n^2}2^r
 =\frac{r2^r}{n},
 \qquad
 M=\frac{w_l}{q_l}=\frac{r2^r}{n}=S.
\tag{20}
\]
Since \(S>0\), the no-dominance inequality is equivalent, after
division by \(\sqrt S\) and squaring, to
\[
 S\log(1/\alpha)\le c_0^2,
\]
which becomes the displayed condition after (20).  Substitution of
(20) into \(\mathrm{thm{:}no\text{-}dominance\text{-}upper}\) proves
the asserted risk bound.  The only confidence restriction used is
\(0<\alpha\le1/4\), together with that displayed no-dominance
condition, so no further extreme-confidence cutoff is present.

added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Write \(\mathsf A=\omega_\alpha(w,q)\).  The partition assumption and
the definition \(w_l=r_l/n\) give
\[
 w_l>0,\qquad \sum_{l=1}^Lw_l=1.
\tag{1}
\]
Also \(q_l=2^{-r_l}\in(0,1/2]\).  The feasible set in
\(\mathrm{def{:}capped\text{-}modulus}\) is a nonempty compact subset
of \([0,1]^L\), and its objective is continuous.  It therefore has an
optimizer \(\delta^*\).  Since all \(w_l\) are positive and \(x>0\),
\(\mathsf A>0\).  Define
\[
 H=\{l:\delta_l^*\ge \mathsf A/2\},
 \qquad W_H=\sum_{l\in H}w_l,
 \qquad Q_H=\sum_{l\in H}q_l.
\]
Feasibility of \(\delta^*\) yields
\[
 Q_H\frac{\mathsf A^2}{4}
 \le \sum_{l\in H}q_l(\delta_l^*)^2
 \le x,
 \qquad  ext{hence}\qquad
 Q_H\le \frac{4x}{\mathsf A^2}.
\tag{2}
\]
On the other hand, (1), \(0\le\delta_l^*\le1\), and the definition of
\(H\) give
\[
 \mathsf A=\sum_lw_l\delta_l^*
 \le W_H+\frac{\mathsf A}{2}\sum_{l\notin H}w_l
 \le W_H+\frac{\mathsf A}{2},
\]
so
\[
 W_H\ge \frac{\mathsf A}{2}.
\tag{3}
\]

We next partition \(H\) into groups of reveal mass at most \(1/2\).
First make every coordinate with \(q_l>1/4\) a singleton group.  Then
order all remaining coordinates arbitrarily and accumulate them until
the running mass first reaches \(1/4\), close that group, and continue.
Each closed group has mass in \([1/4,1/2]\), and only the final group
formed from the remaining coordinates can have mass below \(1/4\).
Thus every group except possibly one has mass at least \(1/4\).  If
\(N\) is the number of groups, then
\[
 N\le4Q_H+1\le\frac{16x}{\mathsf A^2}+1
\tag{4}
\]
by (2).  Thus some group \(G\subseteq H\), with
\(Q_G=\sum_{l\in G}q_l\le1/2\), has weight
\[
 g:=\sum_{l\in G}w_l
 \ge\frac{W_H}{N}
 \ge\frac{\mathsf A^3}{32x+2\mathsf A^2}.
\tag{5}
\]

Fix any measurable \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\).  For each
\(u\in[-1/2,1/2]\), construct a fixed schedule \(m_u\) by setting, for
\(i\in B_l\),
\[
 Y_i^u(d)=
 \begin{cases}
 u,&l\in G\text{ and }d=a,\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\tag{6}
\]
The schedule is nonrandom, respects the block-exposure map, and all
its outcomes lie in \([-1/2,1/2]\); hence the partition, balanced
randomization, fixed-schedule, block-exposure, and bounded-outcome
assumptions imply \(m_u\in\mathcal M_n(B)\).  By
\(\mathrm{def{:}block\text{-}means}\) and the definition of the causal
target,
\[
 \theta(m_u)=gu.
\tag{7}
\]

Let \(\mathsf U_0\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[-1/2,1/2]\) be independent
of \((Z,R)\), and mix the fixed schedules in (6) over \(u=\mathsf U_0\).
This mixing is only a proof device: honesty is applied first to every
fixed \(m_u\).  Let
\[
 \mathcal E_0=\bigcap_{l\in G}\{A_l=0\}.
\]
Disjointness of the blocks and balanced independent assignment imply
that the \(A_l\), \(l\in G\), are independent Bernoulli variables with
success probabilities \(q_l\).  In particular, the union bound gives
\[
 p_0:=P_Z(\mathcal E_0)
 =\prod_{l\in G}(1-q_l)
 \ge1-\sum_{l\in G}q_l
 \ge\frac12.
\tag{8}
\]
On \(\mathcal E_0\), no block in \(G\) attains exposure \(a\), so (6)
and the block-exposure assumption give \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=0\) for
every unit.  Consequently the conditional law of \((D,R)\) on
\(\mathcal E_0\) is independent of \(\mathsf U_0\); this also uses the
declared independence of the external randomizer \(R\).

Uniform honesty and (7), integrated over \(\mathsf U_0\), imply
\[
 P\{g\mathsf U_0\in\Gamma(D,R)\}\ge1-\alpha.
\tag{9}
\]
Combining (8)--(9),
\[
 P\{\mathcal E_0,\ g\mathsf U_0\in\Gamma(D,R)\}
 \ge p_0-\alpha.
\tag{10}
\]
Conditionally on \((\mathcal E_0,D,R)\), the variable
\(g\mathsf U_0\) is uniform on \([-g/2,g/2]\).  For every interval
\(J\), including a random interval after conditioning,
\[
 P\{g\mathsf U_0\in J\mid J\}
 =\frac{\operatorname{len}(J\cap[-g/2,g/2])}{g}
 \le\frac{\operatorname{len}(J)}{g}.
\tag{11}
\]
Equations (10)--(11) therefore give
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[\operatorname{len}\{\Gamma(D,R)\}\right]
 \ge g(p_0-\alpha)
 \ge\frac g4,
\tag{12}
\]
where the expectation on the left averages the fixed-schedule risks
over \(\mathsf U_0\).  Hence the supremum of those risks over
\(m\in\mathcal M_n(B)\) is at least the same quantity.  Taking the
infimum over \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\), then applying (5), proves
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \ge\frac{\mathsf A^3}{128x+8\mathsf A^2}.
\tag{13}
\]
Finally, (1) and \(0\le\delta_l^*\le1\) imply
\(\mathsf A\le1\), while \(x\ge\log4>1\).  Thus
\(128x+8\mathsf A^2\le136x\), and the second inequality follows from
(13).
added_lemmas.justification: A common-location prior on a greedily selected low-reveal group yields a fully finite-sample all-procedure converse strong enough to characterize consistency.
added_lemmas.gap: The cubic dependence on \(\omega_\alpha(w,q)\) is sufficient for the zero-versus-nonzero boundary but does not give the conjectured sharp linear confidence-length modulus.
added_lemmas.consumer: The consistency theorem uses this lower bound to prove that vanishing minimax expected length forces the capped modulus to vanish.

added_lemmas.statement:
There exist universal constants \(c_0,C_1>0\) such that, for every
\(0<\alpha\le1/4\),
\[
 M\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}\le c_0\sqrt S
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le C_1\min\{1,\sqrt{S\log(1/\alpha)}\}.
\]
The infimum defining \(\mathcal R_\alpha\) may range over every
measurable interval procedure randomized by \(R\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\) and \(y=\log(2/\alpha)\).  Since
\(\alpha\le1/4\), one has \(x\ge\log4\) and therefore
\[
 y=x+\log2\le\frac32x.
\tag{14}
\]
By \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}upper}\), the deterministic
observed-data interval \(I_{\mathrm{HT},\alpha}\) is an element of
\(\mathfrak C_\alpha\) and has, under every fixed schedule, pointwise
length at most
\[
 2\min\left\{1,\sqrt{Sy}+\frac{My}{3}\right\}.
\tag{15}
\]
The definition of \(\mathcal R_\alpha\) permits this deterministic
rule even though it also permits rules using the independent
randomizer \(R\).  Hence (15) bounds the minimax risk from above.

Take \(c_0=1\).  Under the displayed no-dominance condition, (14)
implies
\[
 \sqrt{Sy}+\frac{My}{3}
 \le\sqrt{\frac32}\sqrt{Sx}+\frac12M x
 \le\left(\sqrt{\frac32}+\frac12\right)\sqrt{Sx}.
\tag{16}
\]
For \(K\ge1\) and \(z\ge0\),
\(\min\{1,Kz\}\le K\min\{1,z\}\).  Applying this elementary
inequality to (15)--(16), with
\(K=\sqrt{3/2}+1/2\), proves the result with
\[
 C_1=2\left(\sqrt{\frac32}+\frac12\right).
\]
added_lemmas.justification: This theorem records exactly the proved confidence-sensitive upper frontier under the no-dominant-block condition.
added_lemmas.gap: A matching lower bound of linear order in \(\min\{1,\sqrt{S\log(1/\alpha)}\}\) remains the weighted-erasure interval-spread question.
added_lemmas.consumer: The result supplies an honest attainable precision benchmark for heterogeneous school, village, and network partitions.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
Let \(B^{(k)}\) contain \(k\) blocks of size two and \(k\) blocks of
size four, so \(n=6k\).  The two strata have
\((w_l,q_l)=(1/(3k),1/4)\) and
\((w_l,q_l)=(2/(3k),1/16)\), respectively, and
\[
 S=\frac{68}{9k},\qquad M=\frac{32}{3k},\qquad
 \frac{M\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}}{\sqrt S}
 =\frac{32\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}}{\sqrt{68k}}.
\]
Thus, for every fixed \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), the no-dominance condition
holds for all sufficiently large \(k\).  With \(C_1\) denoting the
universal constant in
\(\mathrm{thm{:}no\text{-}dominance\text{-}upper}\),
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le C_1\min\left\{1,
       \sqrt{\frac{68\log(1/\alpha)}{9k}}\right\}
 =O_\alpha(k^{-1/2}).
\]
The two water-filling breakpoints \(q_l/w_l\) are \(3k/4\) and
\(3k/32\).  No common block size can reproduce both reveal
probabilities, or both breakpoints.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The exact two-stratum algebra and attainable upper rate are proved, but the former two-sided minimax-order language depended on the unresolved linear weighted-erasure converse.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
If \(r_l=r\) for every \(l\), then
\[
 L=\frac nr,\qquad q_l=2^{-r},\qquad w_l=\frac rn,
 \qquad S=M=\frac{r2^r}{n}.
\]
With \(c_0,C_1\) denoting the universal constants in
\(\mathrm{thm{:}no\text{-}dominance\text{-}upper}\), the no-dominance
condition is equivalent to
\[
 \frac{r2^r\log(1/\alpha)}{n}\le c_0^2.
\]
Whenever this condition holds, for every \(0<\alpha\le1/4\),
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le C_1\min\left\{1,
       \sqrt{\frac{r2^r\log(1/\alpha)}{n}}\right\}.
\]
Thus the heterogeneous upper theorem recovers the familiar
equal-block effective-count upper rate without any additional
extreme-confidence cutoff.
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The equal-block identities and confidence-length upper bound are proved, whereas the former matching lower-order language depended on the unresolved linear weighted-erasure converse.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The two-sided theorem contains an unproved lower half.  The replacement retains exactly the proved upper half under a name that does not imply a matching converse.

prose_updates.tldr: Unequal clique sizes turn full-neighborhood treatment and control exposure into independent nonidentical categorical reveals.  The observed-data block Horvitz--Thompson estimator has a clipped finite-sample Bernstein interval, and trimming is within a universal constant of the capped water-filling modulus.  A new common-location no-reveal argument, valid for every measurable externally randomized interval, proves \(\mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)\ge \omega_\alpha(w,q)^3/(136\log(1/\alpha))\).  This cubic converse closes the exact consistency boundary \(\mathcal R_\alpha\to0\Longleftrightarrow\omega_\alpha\to0\Longleftrightarrow\rho_0\to0\), including arrays for which \(S\not\to0\).  It does not prove sharp confidence length: the former two-sided no-dominance theorem is replaced by its proved upper half, and the equal- and two-scale corollaries now state upper bounds only.  The sole remaining frontier obstruction is a universal linear weighted-erasure interval-spread converse.  The pinned \(\texttt{szonszein/interference}\) version \(0.1.0\) diagnostic separately reports graph rejection and package-versus-reference label mismatch.

project_justification.gap: Existing partial-interference confidence procedures do not characterize worst-case expected length over every measurable externally randomized interval under fixed balanced assignment on unequal cliques.  The consistency boundary is now settled by a cubic capped-erasure lower bound.  The remaining sharp-frontier gap is singular: strengthen weighted-erasure interval spread from the proved cubic modulus to a universal linear modulus, with the tilted-sign no-dominance and capped global formulations as its two regimes.
project_justification.niche: The paper treats the known assignment distribution as the sole source of randomness and exposes two computable design scales: the quadratic rare-exposure scale for the implementable Bernstein interval and the capped water-filling or trimming scale under dominance.  The capped scale is now necessary and sufficient for consistency, while its sharp linear minimax confidence-length interpretation remains open.
project_justification.fill: The proved portion consists of the exact independent categorical block reduction, an observed-data Horvitz--Thompson estimator, a clipped Bernstein interval, a bias-protected trimmed interval, a certified capped water-filling optimizer, a constant-factor trimming dual, an exact randomized-decision embedding, and a common-location no-reveal lower bound.  Together these results give the full consistency boundary and show that \(S\to0\) is sufficient but not necessary.  The note makes only one-sided sharp-rate claims until a universal linear weighted-erasure converse is proved.

prose_updates.related_work: TchetgenTchetgenVanderWeele2012, Section 4.3, derives finite-sample Hoeffding-type intervals for allocation-strategy effects under a two-stage partial-interference design, and RigdonHudgens2015 obtains exact confidence sets for those effects by randomization-test inversion.  Those estimands and designs differ from the fixed unequal-clique All Treat versus All Control contrast here.  AronowSamii2017 supplies the design--exposure--estimand architecture and exposure-specific inverse weighting, while UganderKarrerBackstromKleinberg2013 shows that full-neighborhood exposure probabilities may be exponentially small in degree.  BasseAiroldi2018 gives a nonconcentration warning, UganderYin2023 changes the design to mitigate small probabilities, and KandirosHarshawSavje2026 studies design-based mean-squared-error criteria rather than all-interval confidence length.  CaiLow2004 and ArmstrongKolesar2018 motivate modulus logic in Gaussian experiments, but do not supply the heterogeneous weighted-erasure interval-spread converse required here.  The new self-contained common-location argument proves the cubic lower bound needed for consistency; it is not presented as the still-missing linear sharp converse.  The pinned \(\texttt{szonszein/interference}\) version \(0.1.0\) source uses the complement of All Treat in its second output column, so the diagnostic compares it with an independently recomputed unanimous All Control reference.
prose_updates.interpretation: The computable quantity \(\rho_0(w,q)\), equivalently the unit-budget capped modulus \(\omega_1(w,q)\), is the correct consistency diagnostic.  A rare block may make \(S\) stay bounded away from zero while carrying so little causal weight that trimming it still permits vanishing honest length.  The cubic lower bound proves that no measurable randomized interval can evade a nonvanishing capped modulus, but its constants and exponent do not determine the sharp finite-confidence length.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The proved common-location construction yields \(\mathcal R_\alpha\gtrsim\omega_\alpha^3/\log(1/\alpha)\), which is exactly strong enough for the fixed-confidence consistency equivalence but can be much smaller than \(\omega_\alpha\).  The no-dominance lower half and the unrestricted sharp capped lower bound therefore remain open manifestations of one problem: a universal linear weighted-erasure interval-spread converse.  Any resolution must control the relevant posterior or concentration function, compact-support boundaries, random reveal information, and external interval randomization; the exact embedding and the cubic no-reveal argument do not supply that missing linear step.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The proved results concern fixed outcomes in \([-1/2,1/2]\), known unequal disjoint clique blocks, and independent unit-level \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) assignment.  The estimator and upper intervals are measurable from \(D\) and known design quantities.  The capped optimizer, trimming comparison, exact consistency boundary, and cubic all-procedure lower bound include arbitrary independent external interval randomization.  Sharp two-sided confidence-length rates are not claimed: under no dominance the note proves the Bernstein upper rate only, and the equal- and two-scale examples inherit only that upper conclusion.  Overlapping or nonclique neighborhoods are rejected before the software diagnostic reports an interval.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), and write \(x=\log(1/\alpha)>1\).  For this
proof let
\[
 \omega_z(w,q)
 :=\max\left\{\sum_lw_l\delta_l:
       0\le\delta_l\le1,\ \sum_lq_l\delta_l^2\le z\right\}.
\tag{16}
\]
Thus \(\omega_\alpha=\omega_x\), while \(\omega_1\) is the budget-one
quantity in \(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\).
Monotonicity of the feasible sets gives \(\omega_1\le\omega_x\).
Conversely, if \(\delta\) is feasible at budget \(x\), then
\(\delta/\sqrt{x}\in[0,1]^L\) and
\[
 \sum_lq_l\left(\frac{\delta_l}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^2\le1.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \omega_1\le\omega_\alpha\le\sqrt{x}\,\omega_1.
\tag{17}
\]
The budget-one part of
\(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\) states
\[
 \omega_1\le\rho_0\le3\omega_1.
\tag{18}
\]
Because \(x\) is fixed, (17)--(18) show, along every triangular array,
\[
 \omega_\alpha\longrightarrow0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \rho_0\longrightarrow0.
\tag{19}
\]

By \(\mathrm{thm{:}trimmed\text{-}upper}\), one honest interval has
pointwise length at most \(2\min\{1,\rho_\alpha\}\).  Taking its
worst-case expectation and then using the confidence-level comparison
in \(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}trimming\text{-}duality}\) yields
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \le2\min\{1,\rho_\alpha(w,q)\}
 \le2\rho_\alpha(w,q)
 \le8\omega_\alpha(w,q).
\tag{20}
\]
Hence \(\omega_\alpha\to0\) implies \(\mathcal R_\alpha\to0\).  In the
opposite direction,
\(\mathrm{lem{:}capped\text{-}erasure\text{-}consistency\text{-}lower}\)
gives at every row of the array
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \ge\frac{\omega_\alpha(w,q)^3}{136x}.
\tag{21}
\]
Since \(x\) is fixed and positive, (21) shows that
\(\mathcal R_\alpha\to0\) implies \(\omega_\alpha\to0\).  Combining
(19)--(21) proves all three equivalences.

It remains to establish the assertion about \(S\).  For every feasible
\(\delta\) at budget \(x\), Cauchy--Schwarz and positivity of \(q_l\)
give
\[
 \sum_lw_l\delta_l
 =\sum_l\frac{w_l}{\sqrt{q_l}}\sqrt{q_l}\delta_l
 \le
 \left(\sum_l\frac{w_l^2}{q_l}\right)^{1/2}
 \left(\sum_lq_l\delta_l^2\right)^{1/2}
 \le\sqrt{xS}.
\tag{22}
\]
Taking the maximum proves \(\omega_\alpha\le\sqrt{xS}\).  Thus
\(S\to0\) is sufficient for consistency by (20).

To show that it is not necessary, for every integer \(k\ge1\) set
\(n_k=2k\,2^k\).  Partition the \(n_k\) units into one block of size
\(2k\) and \(n_k-2k\) singleton blocks, and use the stipulated balanced
Bernoulli design.  The large block has
\[
 w_{\mathrm{big}}=\frac{2k}{n_k}=2^{-k},
 \qquad q_{\mathrm{big}}=2^{-2k},
 \qquad
 \frac{w_{\mathrm{big}}^2}{q_{\mathrm{big}}}=1.
\tag{23}
\]
Each singleton has \(w=1/n_k\) and \(q=1/2\), so
\[
 S^{(n_k)}
 =1+\frac{2(n_k-2k)}{n_k^2}
 \longrightarrow1.
\tag{24}
\]
Let \(J_k\) contain exactly the singleton blocks and put
\(y=\log(2/\alpha)\).  This deterministic choice is admissible in
\(\mathrm{def{:}trimmed\text{-}radius}\), and it gives
\[
 \rho_\alpha(w^{(n_k)},q^{(n_k)})
 \le 2^{-k}
 +\sqrt{\frac{2y(n_k-2k)}{n_k^2}}
 +\frac{2y}{3n_k}
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{25}
\]
Applying \(\mathrm{thm{:}trimmed\text{-}upper}\) to (25) gives
\(\mathcal R_\alpha(w^{(n_k)},q^{(n_k)})\to0\), whereas (24) shows
that \(S^{(n_k)}\not\to0\).  This is the required valid unequal-clique
triangular-array witness.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(0<\alpha\le 1/4\), let \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\), and put
\(A=\omega_\alpha(w,q)\).  Then every uniformly randomization-valid,
possibly externally randomized interval satisfies
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w,q)
 \ge \frac{A^3}{128x+8A^2}
 \ge \frac{A^3}{136x}.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix an arbitrary \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\).  By
\(\mathrm{ass{:}partition}\), every \(r_l\) is positive and
\[
 w_l>0,\qquad \sum_{l=1}^L w_l=1.
\tag{1}
\]
Also \(0<q_l\le 1/2\), because \(q_l=2^{-r_l}\).  The feasible set in
\(\mathrm{def{:}capped\text{-}modulus}\) is a nonempty compact subset
of \([0,1]^L\), so the continuous objective has an optimizer
\(\delta^*\).  Write
\[
 A=\sum_{l=1}^L w_l\delta_l^*,\qquad
 H=\{l:\delta_l^*\ge A/2\}.
\tag{2}
\]
Positivity in (1) and \(x>0\) imply \(A>0\), while (1) and
\(0\le\delta_l^*\le1\) imply \(A\le1\).  On \(H^c\),
\(\delta_l^*<A/2\); hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A
 &=\sum_{l\in H}w_l\delta_l^*
   +\sum_{l\notin H}w_l\delta_l^*\\
 &<\sum_{l\in H}w_l+\frac A2\sum_{l\notin H}w_l
 \le \sum_{l\in H}w_l+\frac A2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \sum_{l\in H}w_l\ge \frac A2.
\tag{3}
\]
Feasibility of \(\delta^*\) and the definition of \(H\) also give
\[
 \frac{A^2}{4}\sum_{l\in H}q_l
 \le\sum_{l\in H}q_l(\delta_l^*)^2
 \le x,
\qquad
 \sum_{l\in H}q_l\le\frac{4x}{A^2}.
\tag{4}
\]

We next partition \(H\) into groups of \(q\)-mass at most \(1/2\).
List its elements in any fixed order and use next-fit packing: keep
adding elements to the current group until the next element would
make its mass exceed \(1/2\), and then start a new group.  This is
feasible because every \(q_l\le1/2\).  If the resulting nonempty
groups have masses \(s_1,\ldots,s_K\), then for every \(j<K\), the
first element placed in group \(j+1\) did not fit in group \(j\).
It follows that \(s_j+s_{j+1}>1/2\).  Therefore
\[
 \frac{K-1}{2}
 <\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}(s_j+s_{j+1})
 \le2\sum_{l\in H}q_l,
\]
and (4) yields
\[
 K\le 4\sum_{l\in H}q_l+1
 \le\frac{16x}{A^2}+1.
\tag{5}
\]
By (3), one group \(G\) has weight
\[
 W:=\sum_{l\in G}w_l
 \ge \frac{A/2}{16x/A^2+1}
 =\frac{A^3}{32x+2A^2},
\qquad
 \sum_{l\in G}q_l\le\frac12.
\tag{6}
\]

For each fixed \(u\in[-1/2,1/2]\), construct a schedule \(m_u\) by
setting, for \(i\in B_l\),
\[
 Y_i^{(u)}(a)=u\ \text{ if }l\in G,
 \qquad
 Y_i^{(u)}(d)=0\ \text{ in every other case}.
\tag{7}
\]
Here the second clause covers \(d\ne a\) in a selected block and every
exposure in an unselected block.  Equation (7) is block homogeneous,
is fixed under \(P_Z\), and lies in \([-1/2,1/2]\).  Together with
\(\mathrm{ass{:}partition}\),
\(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}bernoulli}\), and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}block\text{-}exposure}\), it therefore defines an
element \(m_u\in\mathcal M_n(B)\).  Its causal target is
\[
 \theta(m_u)
 =\sum_{l\in G}w_l\{u-0\}=Wu.
\tag{8}
\]

Introduce only for the Bayes averaging argument a random variable
\(\mathsf U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[-1/2,1/2]\), independently of
\((Z,R)\), and conditionally use schedule \(m_{\mathsf U}\).  Let
\[
 E_0=\bigcap_{l\in G}\{A_l=0\}.
\]
Disjointness of the blocks and independent Bernoulli assignment give
independence of the events \(\{A_l=1\}\), each of probability \(q_l\).
Thus, writing \(p_0=P_Z(E_0)\), the union bound and (6) imply
\[
 p_0=\prod_{l\in G}(1-q_l)
 \ge1-\sum_{l\in G}q_l
 \ge\frac12.
\tag{9}
\]
On \(E_0\), no selected block has exposure \(a\); by (7) every observed
outcome is then zero.  The conditional law of \(Z\) given \(E_0\) does
not involve \(\mathsf U\), and the external randomizer \(R\) is
independent of both.  Hence, conditional on \(E_0\), the data-randomizer
pair \((D,R)\), and therefore \(\Gamma(D,R)\), is independent of
\(\mathsf U\).

Uniform honesty in \(\mathrm{def{:}honest\text{-}intervals}\), applied
separately to every fixed schedule \(m_u\), and then integrated over
\(u\), gives
\[
 \overline P\{W\mathsf U\in\Gamma(D,R)\}\ge1-\alpha,
\tag{10}
\]
where \(\overline P\) is the joint law in the preceding Bayes
experiment.  Therefore
\[
 \overline P\{W\mathsf U\in\Gamma(D,R),E_0\}
 \ge p_0-\alpha.
\tag{11}
\]
Conditional on \(E_0,D,R\), the variable \(W\mathsf U\) is uniform on
\([-W/2,W/2]\).  For every realized measurable interval \(I\),
\[
 P\{W\mathsf U\in I\mid E_0,D,R\}
 =\frac{\operatorname{len}(I\cap[-W/2,W/2])}{W}
 \le\frac{\operatorname{len}(I)}{W}.
\tag{12}
\]
Equations (11)--(12) consequently imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 p_0-\alpha
 &\le \frac1W\,
   \overline{\mathbb E}\!\left[
      \mathbf 1_{E_0}\operatorname{len}\{\Gamma(D,R)\}\right]\\
 &\le \frac1W\,
   \overline{\mathbb E}\!\left[
      \operatorname{len}\{\Gamma(D,R)\}\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
This argument explicitly retains the external randomizer \(R\);
no determinism of the interval rule was used.  By (9),
\(\alpha\le1/4\), and (6),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sup_{m\in\mathcal M_n(B)}
   \mathbb E_{Z,R,m}\operatorname{len}\{\Gamma(D,R)\}
 &\ge \int_{-1/2}^{1/2}
      \mathbb E_{Z,R,m_u}\operatorname{len}\{\Gamma(D,R)\}\,du\\
 &\ge W(p_0-\alpha)
 \ge\frac W4
 \ge\frac{A^3}{128x+8A^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
Taking the infimum over \(\Gamma\in\mathfrak C_\alpha\) proves the
first asserted inequality by \(\mathrm{def{:}length\text{-}risk}\).
Finally \(A\le1\) and \(x=\log(1/\alpha)\ge\log4>1\), so
\[
 128x+8A^2\le136x.
\tag{15}
\]
Combining (14)--(15) proves the second inequality.
added_lemmas.justification: A common-location prior on a greedily selected low-reveal group yields a finite-sample all-procedure converse strong enough to characterize consistency.
added_lemmas.gap: The cubic dependence on \(\omega_\alpha(w,q)\) establishes the consistency boundary but not the conjectured sharp linear confidence-length modulus.
added_lemmas.consumer: The consistency theorem uses this lower bound to prove that vanishing minimax expected length forces the capped modulus to vanish.

proposed.statement:
For every triangular array \((B^{(n)},w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\) and every
fixed \(0<\alpha\le1/4\),
\[
 \mathcal R_\alpha(w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\to0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \omega_\alpha(w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\to0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \rho_0(w^{(n)},q^{(n)})\to0.
\]
In particular, \(S^{(n)}\to0\) is sufficient but not necessary.
proposed.justification: The capped-erasure cubic lower bound and the trimmed upper bound prove the full equivalence between vanishing minimax length, vanishing capped modulus, and vanishing trimmed radius.
proposed.gap: This zero-versus-nonzero characterization does not imply the conjectured sharp linear finite-confidence modulus.
proposed.consumer: Designers can use \(\rho_0(w,q)\to0\) as a computable necessary-and-sufficient consistency certificate even when \(S\not\to0\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof replaces the obsolete dependency on the unresolved water-filling OEQ by the proved cubic erasure lower bound, the established capped-trimming duality, and the trimmed upper theorem.
